claims.text: The current TOR-TILD thermodynamic-integration scheme uses empirical EAM reference potentials.
EAM references cannot adequately represent the wide variety of atomic configurations sampled by an ab initio multicomponent liquid.
The proposed intervention is to replace the EAM reference with an MLIP trained on high-temperature ab initio molecular-dynamics configurations of the liquid.
Deep-learning and moment-tensor approaches are candidate methods for constructing the MLIP.
MLIPs can be used for molecular-dynamics calculations associated with melting predictions that would be costly using direct ab initio simulations.
The method applies to equiatomic or near-equiatomic multicomponent HEAs, including HfNbTaTiZr or similar refractory alloys, in both solid and liquid states near melting.
The simulations are to be performed under constant-pressure conditions near the alloy melting point.
The MLIP captures many-body and directional bonding effects in the liquid more completely than the EAM reference.
EAM is characterized as a limited two-body description of the liquid.
More complete representation of liquid configurational space by the MLIP will improve reference–target phase-space overlap.
Training on high-temperature ab initio liquid data will allow the MLIP to reproduce the liquid energy landscape with higher fidelity.
The higher-fidelity MLIP will better reproduce local and collective atomic fluctuations in the liquid.
Better reproduction of liquid fluctuations and the energy landscape will reduce mismatch along the thermodynamic-integration path from the reference to the ab initio target.
MLIP-referenced thermodynamic integration will have less path mismatch than EAM-referenced TOR-TILD.
Reduced path mismatch will improve the accuracy of the resulting free-energy estimates.
The improvement over EAM is expected to be significant, although no numerical reduction is predicted.
Evidence from elemental and binary calculations using MLIPs suggests a meaningful reduction in integration-path mismatch.
The quantitative gain for multicomponent HEAs remains unverified.
The hypothesis can be tested by parallel MLIP- and EAM-referenced thermodynamic integrations on the same HEA near melting, with comparison to an independent ab initio free-energy benchmark.

Failure of the MLIP route to produce a statistically significant reduction in path mismatch or a free energy closer to the independent ab initio benchmark than the EAM route would falsify the hypothesis.
